title: Water a house plant at its roots without wetting its leaves
instruction: Water the plant at its roots, onto the soil, without wetting its leaves. Then put the jug back on its stool, leave the plant's leaves as they were and take both arms back to where they started.
context: Many house plants (and seedlings, and vegetables in a bed) must be watered at the soil, not over the leaves, which rot or scorch when wet; with leaves spread over the pot, one hand holds the foliage aside while the other pours, as in caring for plants at home, in a nursery or in a care home.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases and sideways from the midpoint between them. (1) A terracotta pot 17 cm across and 7.5 cm tall on a saucer, its middle 30 cm forward and 2 cm right of the centre line, filled with dark soil 1.3 cm below its rim; fixed. In it a house plant with a green stem and broad leaves (15 cm long, up to 13 cm wide) spread low over the soil: three fixed in the crown, over the back and both sides of the pot, and one big leaf in front on a springy stalk, joined to the stem 10 cm above the table, lying over the front of the soil and reaching out 6 cm past the rim toward the arms. Pushed round on its stalk, the big leaf springs back over the soil when let go. (2) A blue plastic watering jug (5.4 cm across, 8.5 cm tall, with a pouring lip and a handle) holding 120 ml of water, simulated as 12 drops (7 mm beads, 10 ml each), standing on a beech stool 6 cm tall, 26 cm forward and 13 cm left of the centre line. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot. Real trial: a peace lily (Spathiphyllum, about 25 cm tall) in the same 17 cm terracotta pot on a saucer, its soil just moist, three leaves over the back and sides and one big lower leaf on a flexible stalk lying over the front of the soil; the jug (about 150 ml) filled with 120 ml of room-temperature water.
scoring: Judged at the end. Simulation: a water bead (10 ml) wets a leaf if it ever comes within 4 mm of one; it waters the soil if it lands on the soil inside the pot without having touched a leaf. Real trial: weigh the potted plant with its saucer before and after (1 g per ml) for the water delivered, and blot every leaf with a pre-weighed paper towel for the water on the leaves; water on the soil = the gain minus the blotted water. 1.0 with at least 90 ml on the soil (9 of the 12 beads), at most 10 ml ever on the leaves (1 bead), the jug back on its stool (within 3 cm, upright within 15 degrees), the big leaf back over the soil (within 12 degrees of where it lay), both hands let go (each TCP at least 4 cm from the jug and the leaf) and both arms back where they started (each TCP within 5 cm); 0.5 with at least 90 ml on the soil and at most 10 ml on the leaves; 0.25 with at least 40 ml on the soil (4 beads); else 0.0. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held for 1 s with the jug, the big leaf and every bead still.
reset_notes: Let the pot drain until its soil is just moist again (weigh it back to its starting weight), dry the leaves, lay the big leaf back over the soil, refill the jug to 120 ml and stand it on its stool.
fidelity: Rigid-body simulation (Isaac Sim 6.1, PhysX, 20 Hz control). Simplified: the 120 ml of water is 12 rigid 7 mm beads (10 ml each, 0.8 g) that do not soak in or cling; a real trial weighs the water delivered and blots the leaves. Leaves are rigid plates; the crown's leaves and the pot are fixed, and the big leaf turns on its stalk about the stem against a spring (0.0016 N m per degree).
